name: Deep Vinaceous
lede: Deep Vinaceous is a dusty rose-pink from Ridgway's 1912 chart, sharing its exact hex with the later, separately named Antique Rose.

sections.title: The same pink, two names
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXVII gives this hue the name Deep Vinaceous, hue 1′′, tone b, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the nearest category as "dark pink" in its block 6 [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[marsh-rose]], [[dusty-rose]] and [[copper-penny]], at 4.2, 4.2 and 4.2 ΔE [1]. Our library's exact match in the archive is [[antique-rose]], the identical hex under a later, unrelated name, which shows how two separate naming projects can land on the same pink by different routes [3].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 56, chroma 24, hue 20 degrees, Munsell 2.8R 5.5/5.2 [1]. The nearest distinct color beyond that exact match is [[marsh-rose]], about 4.2 CIEDE2000 units away [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 57 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 0.24 percent, as photographed [4]. It peaks in the 1910s, in 6 of 523 paintings, at 4.8 times the overall rate, and is most loved by Henri Matisse, in four of his fifty paintings here, thirty-three times his own museums' baseline; it most often plays a mid-tone, in 53 percent of its appearances [4].

The earliest dated match is Paolo di Giovanni Fei's *The Presentation of the Virgin in the Temple*, 1398, more than five centuries before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
